question: What does 'asepsis' mean in the hospital?

options.A: The application of antibiotics to a sterile wound
options.B: The boiling of surgical instruments in hot water
options.C: The complete removal of all visible dirt and dust
options.D: The total absence of disease-producing microorganisms

explanation: Asepsis simply means being completely free from germs (pathogens) that can make a patient sick. You've got this! [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h1)

question: Why do nurses worry so much about hospital-acquired infections?

options.A: They are impossible to treat with modern standard drugs
options.B: They automatically lead to the immediate closure of wards
options.C: They only occur in poorly funded government hospitals
options.D: They prolong hospital stays and increase patient suffering

explanation: Infections picked up in the hospital make patients stay longer and suffer more. Preventing them is a huge part of our job! [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h1)

question: Which of these actions is a good example of 'medical asepsis'?

options.A: Reducing the overall number of microorganisms
options.B: Destroying every single bacterial spore on a tray
options.C: Using a flame to sterilize a metal forceps
options.D: Applying concentrated bleach to hospital floors

explanation: Medical asepsis (like regular handwashing) is all about reducing the number of germs so they don't spread. Keep up the good work! [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h2)

question: You are about to pass a urinary catheter for a patient. Which technique must you use?

options.A: Standard cleaning because urine contains normal waste products
options.B: Medical asepsis because the procedure is performed at the bedside
options.C: Surgical asepsis because the urinary tract is normally sterile
options.D: Disinfection technique using warm soapy water and clean towels

explanation: Because the inside of the urinary tract is germ-free, anything entering it must be completely sterile to avoid introducing bacteria. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h2)

question: An unwashed clinical thermometer has bacteria living on it. In the chain of infection, what is this thermometer?
explanation: A reservoir is simply a home where germs live, grow, and hang out waiting to move to someone else! [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h3)

question: How does simple handwashing mainly stop the spread of infection?

options.A: It eliminates the original infectious agent
options.B: It closes the portal of exit permanently
options.C: It interrupts the mode of transmission
options.D: It destroys the susceptibility of the host

explanation: Washing your hands washes away germs, stopping them from traveling from one surface or patient to another. Simple and lifesaving! [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h3)

question: When should you use soap and water instead of an alcohol hand rub?

options.A: Immediately after removing clean non-sterile gloves
options.B: When rushing between multiple patients in a busy ward
options.C: When hands are visibly soiled with dirt or body fluids
options.D: Before taking a patient's routine temperature and pulse

explanation: If your hands have visible dirt or fluids on them, alcohol gels won't work well. Head to the sink for good old soap and water! [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h4)

question: Why do we use standard precautions for every single patient in the ward?

options.A: Infectious status is often unknown or asymptomatic
options.B: Global health bodies prohibit single-room isolations
options.C: Hospital policy mandates testing every admission daily
options.D: Patients get offended if precautions are applied selectively

explanation: You can't always tell who has an infection just by looking at them. Treating everyone with standard precautions keeps you and the patients safe! [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h4)

question: When opening a sterile pack, which part of the wrapper is considered contaminated?

options.A: The bottom half facing the floor
options.D: The exact center of the sheet

explanation: Your hands have to touch the outer edges to open the pack, so we consider that outer one-inch border contaminated. Good to know for your clinicals! [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h5)

question: A sterile instrument slips and drops below your waist level. What should you do?

options.A: Discard the forceps and replace it immediately
options.B: Use it only if the patient has a clean wound
options.C: Lift the instrument back up onto the sterile tray
options.D: Wipe the instrument with spirit and reuse it

explanation: Once an item drops below your waist, it is out of your sight line and no longer considered sterile. Toss it and grab a fresh one! [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h5)

question: What must you always do before you disinfect or sterilize a dirty instrument?
explanation: You can't sterilize dirt! Washing off blood and tissue first is a must so the heat or chemicals can actually reach the germs. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h6)

question: Why is autoclaving better than simply boiling instruments in water?

options.A: Boiling water only removes visible dirt and dust
options.B: High pressure cools down the metal faster after use
options.C: Autoclaves prevent metal instruments from rusting
options.D: Steam under pressure destroys resistant bacterial spores

explanation: An autoclave uses pressurized steam to reach super-high temperatures that kill tough bacterial spores which regular boiling water can't defeat. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h6)

question: What is your best response if you see a colleague accidentally break a sterile field?

options.A: Wait until the procedure ends before filing a report
options.B: Stop the procedure and correct the contamination immediately
options.C: Ask the junior staff member to clean the floor later
options.D: Ignore the mistake if the patient appears healthy

explanation: Patient safety comes first! Always speak up right away to prevent introducing germs into a vulnerable patient. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h7)

question: Which of these actions is completely WRONG in a clinical setting?

options.A: Reusing disposable syringes after washing them in hot water
options.B: Checking expiry dates on sterile packaging before opening
options.C: Segregating infectious waste into correct color-coded bins
options.D: Challenging lapses in infection control among ward staff

explanation: Disposable items are strictly single-use! Washing and reusing them is dangerous and puts patients at huge risk of severe infections. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h7)
